summary:
Earth Jukebox: Hearing Our Changing Planet

NASA's Earth Information Center visualizations are almost entirely visual, which leaves blind and low-vision users out of Earth science. Earth Jukebox is a web app that turns EIC images and animations into music, so anyone can listen to the planet.
The app scans each frame from left to right. Brightness sets pitch, color saturation sets loudness, and the dominant hue chooses the harmony. Dark areas stay silent, busy textures add extra notes, and sound pans across the stereo field as the scan moves. Notes come from pentatonic scales, so the result stays musical: warm images use a bright major scale, cool images a darker minor one. In video mode, the music updates continuously as the visualization plays.

Accessibility is central. The app supports screen readers and full keyboard control, offers editable image descriptions, and speaks a live description of what is being heard. Users can also export any sonification as a WAV file.
Everything runs in the browser with no installation, using the Web Audio API. All visuals are credited to NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio.
details:
**Project Details**

**What it does**

Earth Jukebox translates NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) visualizations into sound, so people who cannot see the images can still explore Earth science. Users pick a frame or load a video, press play, and hear a soundscape generated in real time from the pixels. The result can also be saved as an audio file.

**How sight becomes sound**

The app scans each image from left to right, and left-to-right position becomes time and stereo position. For every column of pixels it measures brightness, color saturation, hue, and texture.

- Brightness sets pitch: bright areas are high notes, dark areas are low notes, and very dark areas are silent.

- Saturation sets loudness: vivid colors are louder.

- Hue chooses the chord that plays underneath.

- The darkness of the lower part of the image sets a deep bass note.

- Sharp changes in the image (edges, texture) add extra notes, so busy regions sound busier.

- Very bright upper areas, such as ice and clouds, add a high shimmer.

All notes come from pentatonic scales so the result is pleasant to listen to. Warm-colored images use a bright major scale, and cool-colored images use a darker minor scale. In video mode, a snapshot of the playing video is analyzed every 0.8 seconds and split into four strips. Each strip becomes one note, so the music changes as the planet changes.

**Accessibility**

- Works with screen readers and is fully keyboard-operable (Space to play/stop, arrow keys to change frame, D to read the description).

- Every image has an editable text description, and a live text description of the current section is announced during playback.

- A written explanation of the sight-to-sound mapping is on the page, so listeners know what they are hearing.

**Technology**

HTML, JavaScript, Canvas (pixel analysis) and the Web Audio API (synthesis, reverb, stereo panning). It runs entirely in the browser with no server, installation, or machine learning model, so anyone can open it on a laptop. Audio export uses an offline audio renderer and writes standard WAV files.

**NASA data used**

[List the items you actually used, for example: Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature (SVS 3912), Change in Night Lights 2012-2023 (SVS 5313), Air Quality Model Runs (SVS 5533).] All visuals are credited to NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio and the Earth Information Center.

**Creative choices**

We chose to make the mapping predictable instead of random, so a listener can learn it: higher means brighter, left to right means time. We limited the notes to musical scales so the sound is engaging instead of noisy, and we chose a gentle, slow tempo so the images feel exploratory, not alarming.
